The source rejects the excuse that a product is too dull, holding that there are no dull products only dull writers, and reports never assigning a product to a writer not personally interested in it, because every bad campaign the author wrote was for a product that did not interest him.

item.rationale: SPEC-01 already assigns each entity a role, with `hero` among the permitted values. This source supplies a rule for filling that field in commercial work: the customer occupies the hero role and the brand occupies a supporting one. A brief that marks the product or the brand as hero and also claims to be customer-centric is a detectable conflict between two fields we already hold.

applicability.when: assigning entity roles for a brand asset intended to persuade a customer
applicability.limits: SPEC-01's `hero` marks the primary visual subject of an asset, while this source's hero is the protagonist of a narrative the customer is living. Those are not the same thing, and a product can be the visual subject of a shot in which the customer is still the protagonist. The rule is usable as a check on the message; it must not be read as forbidding product-led imagery.

item.definition_in_origin_frame: Put the product itself at the centre of the advertising, shown with simplicity.
The differentiation advertising style contributes to a product that is not itself different from its competitors.

source_terms: Framing the shot usually comes before anything else—the first decision.

Composition (or design if you like) covers the whole range of organizing the image, while framing concentrates on enclosing the scene, even before thinking about the relationship between elements inside the picture.
item.claim: Framing and composition are different acts. Framing concentrates on enclosing the scene and comes before anything else, prior even to thinking about relationships between the elements inside the picture; composition covers the whole range of organising the image. The source notes the term comes from filmmaking, where a scene is enclosed and the action then plays out within it, and concedes the separation is less sharp in still photography, where the image is singular rather than multiple. Even so, the decisions about where to cut into a landscape, figure or object, and what to include and leave out, rank as the most important in defining the shot.

mechanism.text: In film the enclosure is fixed first and the action happens inside it, which is what makes framing logically prior. The source imports that ordering into still photography while acknowledging it fits less cleanly.

caveats.text: the source states directly that the separation may not hold to the same degree in still photography
the claim that framing decisions are the most important in defining the shot is asserted and is not revisited or tested anywhere in the three parts

intra_source_relations.note: placing is treated as the next decision after framing
the source says the two are inseparably linked

item.question: What does this source say changed after economic liberalisation, and why is this the object in the record most likely to be out of date?
item.answer: She describes a double movement: 'one set of processes creates identifiable symbols of cultural identity while another lays down the universal ground within which these markers of difference operate.' The mechanism she names in the trade is concrete — 'advertising agencies in India — the new Ravi Varmas, if you will — often use proprietary analytical models from their parent companies overseas, filling in the blanks with content specific to Indian market segments.' With it comes a narrowing of what 'culture' is taken to mean: circumscribed, globally portable signs of heterogeneity — language, dress, food, music, art, rituals, festivals — grafted onto the protocols of a putatively universal modernity, which relegates cultural difference to leisure and harnesses it to niche marketing. IT IS THE MOST DATED OBJECT IN THE RECORD because it is a characterisation of a media landscape observed to roughly 2004-06, drawn largely from one firm's transformation seen at two points, and it precedes the Indian smartphone, cheap mobile data, UPI and streaming entirely — any of which would change the picture materially.
item.support: agencies 'use proprietary analytical models from their parent companies overseas, filling in the blanks with content specific to Indian market segments'
item.confounders: The template-plus-local-content observation is sharp and quotable, which is precisely why its date and its narrow evidence base need to travel with it.

item.question: What does the Woodward's Gripe Water calendar demonstrate, on this reading, and what is the general claim it supports?
item.answer: Jain reads M. V. Dhurandhar's 1932 calendar as deploying TWO DISTINCT REGISTERS OF SIGNIFICATION AT ONCE: a perspectival, narrative, allegorical register aimed at a modernising Indian and European resident elite, and an indexical, frontal, iconic register that institutes a divine presence. A single image addresses two constituencies that read pictures differently, without either being asked to read the other's way. The general claim it supports is that the deployment of new image-making techniques, including technological mass reproduction and elements of Western naturalism, 'helped mass-manufactured images to forge an arena of common address across varying social constituencies — that is, to "naturalize" an expanded category of the popular'. She states the consequence: 'commodity aesthetics provided a ground for reformulations of community and locality', driven by the opposing expansive and conservative imperatives of mass manufacture. This is an art-historical argument about a specific colonial episode, read from one image; it is not a general finding about how images address audiences.
item.support: new techniques 'helped mass-manufactured images to forge an arena of common address across varying social constituencies'
item.confounders: One image, closely read, is the whole evidence for this reading. The reading is careful and the evidential base is a single artefact.

item.visible_content: Four panels in two rows. Left of each row, a poster for the same event — a Hear-Say reading by Henry Magaziner at a Philadelphia bookshop, with the same date, time and address. Right of each row, the alignment structure that composition implies, drawn as teal rules. Top row: the information is set as one flush-right stack, and the derived structure is two fields divided by a single vertical axis. Bottom row: the same information is broken into several differently-weighted groups scattered across the format, and the derived structure is a multi-field grid of roughly five vertical and five horizontal divisions.
item.what_the_visual_supports: That a grid is READ OFF a composition rather than imposed on it. The content is held constant and only the grouping changes, and the structure changes with it. It also supports the source's narrower claim that a large variety of layouts is reachable inside strict limits: both posters use one type family and a small set of sizes.
item.requires_prose: That like information is grouped and disparate information separated, and that changes in weight and scale are what introduce hierarchy. The picture shows the outcome; the caption supplies the rule that produced it.
item.extractor_note: This is the clearest minimal pair in the section — same content, one variable (grouping) changed, both results shown with their derived structures. The caption states the claim, so a text-only extraction keeps the claim and loses the proof.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

item.question: What contrast does the source draw between Indian and contemporary Western posters, and what reason does it give for the Indian side of it?
item.answer: Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which the public must see the film to resolve, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as 'the media seal of approval' plus studio, producer and director credits signalling the film's status. Indian posters 'rarely use text'. The reason given is distribution: with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier' — text picks a language, and picking a language cuts the audience. From the 1980s it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are themselves a marker of the style, content and quality of the film.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: The absence of text is not an aesthetic preference in this account; it is a response to a multilingual distribution constraint, and the three names that DO appear are doing the work the review quotations do elsewhere.

source_terms: text is seen as a cultural barrier
item.claim: Patel states a structural contrast between two poster traditions. Contemporary Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which requires the public to see the film to resolve it, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as "the media seal of approval," plus studio, producer and director credits that signal the film's status. Indian posters, in contrast, "rarely use text": with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, "text is seen as a cultural barrier." From the 1980s onward it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are a marker of the style, content and quality of the film. Indian posters accordingly "convey the familiarity of the form and content of the Indian film" rather than an enigma.

mechanism.text: Text has to be read in a language, so any text narrows the poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory. Where the distribution is wide and the audience already knows the form, the poster's job shifts from posing a question to confirming a familiar promise, and that job can be done by images and by three names.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters from the 1980s onward against contemporary Western practice. Patel notes the earlier Indian convention was different — title and star names prominently in English with Hindi and Urdu titles in smaller lettering nearby — so this too is dated.

caveats.text: the comparison is drawn between two practices as the author characterises them; no sample of Western posters is enumerated and no count is given on either side

Patel notes the cost of the change she documents: more recent designs focusing on one narrative element are 'more universally understood' but 'convey less information about the culture in which they are produced'. That trade-off is stated by the source and is the most useful part of this object

source_stated_problems: text narrows a poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory
source_stated_remedies: carry the message in recognisable images and in the three names that index style, content and quality

positive: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995), three posters each focusing on a strand of the romance
Pardes (1997), an amalgamation with an American cityscape and the Taj Mahal diagonally opposed
